catalog_locator: Ch. IV Phonotactics, sec. 4.2 'Iambic versus trochaic rhythm', p. 156 and sec. 4.4.1 'Phonological reduction of prefixes', p. 170; suffix passage Ch. VI §50c, p. 301.
catalog_quote: [p. 156] There is a major distinction in rhythm between Khispi and Duhumbi on the one hand, and the Sartang and Sherdukpen varieties on the other. Whereas in Khispi and Duhumbi the meter in most words consists of a stressed syllable followed by one or more unstressed syllables, in the Sartang and Sherdukpen varieties an unstressed syllable is followed by a stressed syllable, in other words, the Khispi and Duhumbi rhythm is trochaic, that of the Sartang and Sherdukpen varieties iambic. In trochaic languages, the first syllable of a word tends to be stressed, and hence often long, whereas the second syllable is unstressed, and may or may not be shorter. [...] [p. 170] Khispi and Duhumbi have trochaic rhythm with stress on the first syllable of a word, and thus even stress prefixes, which is why prefixes maintained their full CiV(Cf) syllabic shape. The Sartang and Sherdukpen varieties, on the other hand, obtained iambic rhythm through language contact, stressing the second syllable of a word, which, in the case of prefixed words, is always the root and not the prefix.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Khispi words are trochaic: stress falls on the first syllable of the word (including on a prefix when the word is prefix + root), with following syllables unstressed; this contrasts with the iambic (second-syllable/root-stressed) Sartang and Sherdukpen varieties.
new_statements.exceptions: Hedged as 'in most words'; no Khispi-specific exceptions listed. (For closely related Duhumbi, Bodt's 2018 Zenodo note lists a few stressed suffixes such as -deʔ PRES and -tʰeʔ SUBJ:NPST, but that is stated for Duhumbi, not Khispi.) Sec. 3.2 says Khispi phonology is otherwise like Duhumbi's, for which Bodt (2020, Grammar of Duhumbi; Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.1284478) states stress is non-distinctive and word-initial in di- and polysyllabic words including suffixed forms.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rhythm/stress stated for the (morphological) word, based on elicited lexical items in the Western Kho-Bwa comparative dataset; the statement is made jointly for Khispi and Duhumbi in a comparative-historical monograph rather than in a dedicated Khispi prosody section (sec. 3.2 Khispi has none). No phrase-level discussion for Khispi.
new_statements.identity_note: The source's 'Khispi' is the language Glottolog calls Khispi/Lish (lish1235, ISO lsh), spoken in Lish and associated villages (data mainly from Lish village speakers, e.g. LISH090614B). The stress statement is made jointly for Khispi and its closest relative Duhumbi (Chugpa, chug1252); Bodt treats the two as separate but mutually largely intelligible varieties (sec. 3.2.4).

sources.note: Ch. III sec. 3.2 Khispi (pp. 62-67) gives the inventory only ('Khispi phonology is similar to the Duhumbi phonology'). Ch. IV sec. 4.2 'Iambic versus trochaic rhythm' (pp. 156-158): in Khispi and Duhumbi the meter of most words is a stressed syllable followed by unstressed syllable(s) = trochaic; Sartang/Sherdukpen iambic. Sec. 4.4.1 (p. 170): 'Khispi and Duhumbi have trochaic rhythm with stress on the first syllable of a word, and thus even stress prefixes'.

sources.citation: Bodt, Timotheus Adrianus. 2018. Duhumbi Phonology - Iambic to Trochaic Rhythm? Zenodo, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.1284482 (4-pp. note).
sources.note: Primarily about Duhumbi (trochaic foot, stress on first syllable/prefix); states that Khispi, like Duhumbi, changed from iambic to trochaic rhythm ('the change from iambic to trochaic rhythm in the small and confined languages Khispi and Duhumbi'; 'Duhumbi (and also Khispi) speakers tend to insert epenthetic consonants.. as a result of the change from an iambic to a trochaic foot'), contrasting with Sartang/Sherdukpen 'with stress always on the second syllable of a bisyllabic word'.
